questions.q: A 35-year-old male from rural India presents with a single well-defined hypopigmented patch on the forearm with complete loss of sensation. Slit-skin smear is negative for acid-fast bacilli. Nerve biopsy shows well-formed epithelioid granulomas with Langhans giant cells around dermal nerves. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy (TT) presents with a single or few well-defined, hypopigmented, anaesthetic patches with negative SSS and well-formed epithelioid granulomas around dermal nerves on histology. Strong cell-mediated immunity keeps bacterial load undetectable.

questions.q: A 48-year-old woman presents with painful oral erosions for 3 months, followed by fragile flaccid blisters on the trunk that rupture easily leaving raw erosions. Nikolsky sign is positive. Biopsy shows suprabasal acantholysis just above the basal layer. The primary target autoantigen responsible for this presentation is:
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris with mucosal involvement targets Desmoglein 3 (Dsg3), which is highly expressed in mucosal epithelia. In mucocutaneous PV, both Dsg3 and Dsg1 are targeted. Dsg1 alone causes pemphigus foliaceus (no mucosal involvement).

questions.q: A 72-year-old man presents with tense, non-rupturing blisters on an erythematous base predominantly on the lower abdomen and thighs. Nikolsky sign is negative. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear C3 and IgG deposition along the basement membrane zone. The most likely primary target autoantigen is:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid classically occurs in the elderly with tense blisters and negative Nikolsky sign. The primary target is BP180 (BPAG2/collagen XVII), a hemidesmosomal transmembrane protein. BP230 (BPAG1) is a secondary target. Linear IgG/C3 at BMZ on DIF is characteristic.

questions.q: A 20-year-old presents with hypo- and hyperpigmented macules on the upper trunk that failed to tan uniformly with the rest of the body. KOH examination of skin scrapings shows short hyphae and round spores resembling 'spaghetti and meatballs.' Which statement about the causative organism is MOST accurate?
opts: It is a dermatophyte requiring keratin for growth
It requires exogenous lipids for in vitro culture
Wood's lamp shows brilliant white fluorescence
Topical terbinafine is the most effective treatment
questions.exp: Tinea versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur (and related species), a lipophilic yeast. It lacks fatty acid synthase and therefore requires exogenous lipids for culture (hence growth on olive-oil-enriched media). Wood's lamp shows yellow-green/golden fluorescence, not white (brilliant white = vitiligo). KOH shows the classic 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance.

questions.q: A 26-year-old sexually active male presents with a non-pruritic papulosquamous rash involving the palms and soles, generalized painless lymphadenopathy, and mucous patches in the mouth. He recalls a transient painless genital ulcer that resolved spontaneously 6 weeks ago. RPR is reactive at 1:128. What is the first-line treatment?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
Azithromycin 1g orally as a single dose
questions.exp: This is secondary syphilis (rash on palms/soles, lymphadenopathy, mucous patches following a primary chancre). The treatment of choice for primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis is Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM as a single dose. Doxycycline is an alternative for penicillin-allergic patients.

questions.q: A 74-year-old fair-skinned woman presents with a slowly enlarging, irregularly pigmented macule on her cheek measuring 3.5cm with shades of tan, brown, and dark brown. She has extensive solar elastosis. Dermoscopy shows rhomboid structures, dark circles, and asymmetric follicular pigmentation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Lentigo maligna (melanoma in situ on sun-damaged skin)
questions.exp: Lentigo maligna (LM) is melanoma in situ arising on chronically sun-damaged skin of elderly patients, typically the face. Dermoscopy shows rhomboid structures, annular-granular pattern, and dark circles (obliterated follicular openings). Solar lentigo is uniformly pigmented without atypia. LM may progress to invasive lentigo maligna melanoma.

questions.q: A 45-year-old on carbamazepine for 5 weeks develops high fever, extensive morbilliform eruption covering >50% BSA, facial edema, painful cervical lymphadenopathy, peripheral eosinophilia (1800 cells/uL), and elevated liver enzymes (AST 180 U/L). This clinical picture is most consistent with:
opts: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)
questions.exp: DRESS (Drug Hypersensitivity Syndrome) is characterized by: onset 2-8 weeks after drug initiation, extensive morbilliform rash, facial edema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia ≥1500/uL, atypical lymphocytosis, and internal organ involvement (liver most common). SJS/TEN shows skin detachment/blistering rather than morbilliform rash. Carbamazepine is a classic culprit.

questions.q: A 24-year-old female presents with a butterfly-shaped erythematous rash over both cheeks, photosensitivity, recurrent oral ulcers, and polyarthralgia. ANA is positive at 1:640. Which antibody, if positive, is the MOST SPECIFIC for systemic lupus erythematosus?
questions.exp: Anti-Smith (anti-Sm) antibodies are the most specific for SLE (~99% specificity) though sensitivity is only ~25%. Anti-dsDNA is also highly specific (~97%) and correlates with disease activity/lupus nephritis. Anti-Ro and Anti-La are more characteristic of Sjogren's syndrome, though also seen in SLE.

questions.q: A 42-year-old female presents with Raynaud's phenomenon for 4 years, progressive skin thickening extending to the upper arms and trunk (diffuse pattern), dysphagia, and bilateral basal lung fibrosis on HRCT. Which antibody is most likely to be positive in this patient?
questions.exp: Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc) with interstitial lung disease (ILD) is strongly associated with anti-topoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70). Anti-centromere antibody is seen in limited cutaneous SSc (CREST syndrome) with lower ILD risk. Anti-RNA Pol III is associated with dcSSc and renal crisis. Anti-Jo-1 is seen in antisynthetase syndrome.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with heliotrope rash with periorbital edema, Gottron's papules over the MCPs and PIPs, V-sign erythema on the chest, and proximal muscle weakness. CK is markedly elevated. Which investigation is MOST important to perform urgently in this adult patient?
opts: CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis
questions.exp: Adult dermatomyositis carries a significant risk of associated internal malignancy (15-30%), especially in those over 50 years. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis is the standard first-line investigation for malignancy screening. Common associated malignancies include ovarian, lung, gastric, colorectal, and nasopharyngeal cancers. Anti-TIF1-gamma positivity increases malignancy risk.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male with stable plaque psoriasis develops hypertension. His cardiologist asks for guidance on antihypertensive selection. Which class of antihypertensive is MOST likely to exacerbate or trigger psoriasis?
questions.exp: Beta-blockers are well-recognized triggers and exacerbators of psoriasis. They may worsen psoriasis through mechanisms including reduced cAMP in keratinocytes and altered T-cell function. Lithium is another classic drug causing psoriasis. NSAIDs and antimalarials can also worsen it. CCBs and ACE inhibitors are generally considered safe.

questions.q: A 4-year-old boy has chronic pruritic eczema on the cheeks, wrists, and antecubital fossae since infancy. His father has asthma. Genetic testing reveals a loss-of-function mutation in the FLG gene (filaggrin). This mutation primarily leads to:
opts: Increased filaggrin production and epidermal thickening
Impaired skin barrier, increased transepidermal water loss, and enhanced allergen sensitization
Decreased total IgE and reduced atopic tendency
Defective neutrophil chemotaxis and increased bacterial infections
questions.exp: Filaggrin (encoded by FLG) is critical for skin barrier integrity and natural moisturizing factor production. Loss-of-function mutations cause impaired barrier, increased TEWL, xerosis, and enhanced penetration of allergens and irritants, leading to sensitization and the atopic march (eczema, asthma, allergic rhinitis). FLG mutations are the strongest genetic risk factor for atopic dermatitis.

questions.q: A 35-year-old nurse develops recurrent pruritic vesicular dermatitis on the dorsum of both hands whenever wearing rubber protective gloves. Patch testing to the European Standard Battery shows 2+ positivity to thiuram mix and negative reaction to latex protein. This finding indicates:
opts: Type I IgE-mediated hypersensitivity to natural rubber latex proteins
Type IV delayed hypersensitivity to a rubber vulcanization accelerant
Irritant contact dermatitis from prolonged occlusive glove use
Photoallergic contact dermatitis triggered by UV through glove material
questions.exp: Thiuram mix contains thiuram disulfides, which are accelerants used in the vulcanization of natural rubber. Positivity to thiuram on patch testing indicates Type IV (delayed-type) allergic contact dermatitis to the rubber additive, not to latex protein. True latex allergy (Type I) presents as urticaria/anaphylaxis, not vesicular eczema, and would show positive latex-specific IgE.

questions.q: A 68-year-old diabetic male presents with burning pain along the left T4 dermatome for 3 days followed by grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in the same distribution. He presents within 48 hours of vesicle onset. The most appropriate antiviral treatment is:
opts: Acyclovir 200mg orally five times daily for 7 days
Acyclovir 800mg orally five times daily for 7 days
Valacyclovir 500mg orally twice daily for 5 days
No antiviral required; treat with analgesics only
questions.exp: Herpes zoster requires high-dose acyclovir: 800mg five times daily (every 4 hours, omitting the night dose) for 7-10 days. The standard 200mg dose is for HSV-1/2, not VZV. Valacyclovir for zoster is 1g three times daily (not 500mg twice daily). Antivirals are indicated if started within 72 hours of rash onset, especially in immunocompromised or high-risk patients.

questions.q: A 7-year-old child presents with multiple 2-4mm dome-shaped, umbilicated papules on the trunk, axillae, and behind the knees. The lesions are flesh-colored and non-pruritic. What is the causative organism?
opts: Molluscipoxvirus (a member of the Poxviridae family)
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by Molluscipoxvirus, a double-stranded DNA poxvirus. It spreads by direct skin contact or fomites. The characteristic central umbilication contains a caseous plug with Henderson-Paterson (molluscum) bodies visible on histology.

questions.q: A 23-year-old sexually active male presents with multiple soft, flesh-colored, cauliflower-like papillomatous growths on the penile shaft and perianal region. The HPV subtypes most commonly responsible for these anogenital condylomata acuminata are:
questions.exp: HPV 6 and 11 are low-risk (non-oncogenic) subtypes responsible for >90% of anogenital warts (condylomata acuminata) and recurrent respiratory papillomatosis. HPV 16 and 18 are high-risk oncogenic subtypes associated with cervical, oropharyngeal, anal, and penile carcinomas. The quadrivalent HPV vaccine (Gardasil) covers subtypes 6, 11, 16, and 18.

questions.q: A 65-year-old man presents with a pearly, translucent nodule with prominent telangiectasias on the nasal ala. It has a rolled (pearly) border and a central area of ulceration. The most common histological subtype of basal cell carcinoma is:
questions.exp: Nodular BCC is the most common histological subtype, accounting for approximately 60-70% of all BCCs. It shows islands of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and retraction artifact. Morpheaform/sclerosing BCC has the highest recurrence rate after standard excision. Superficial BCC is most common on the trunk.

questions.q: A 65-year-old farmer presents with a firm, hyperkeratotic, slowly enlarging nodule on the lower lip vermilion for 3 months. Biopsy confirms well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. Which precancerous lesion most commonly precedes lip SCC?
questions.exp: Actinic cheilitis (solar cheilosis) is the most common precursor for SCC on the lower lip vermilion and is caused by chronic cumulative UV radiation exposure. It presents as blurring of the vermilion border, dryness, scaling, and atrophy. Up to 10-20% may transform to SCC. Outdoor workers (farmers, fishermen) are at highest risk.

questions.q: A 58-year-old male has had persistent itchy scaly patches and indurated plaques on the buttocks and trunk for 12 years. Biopsy shows epidermotropism of atypical lymphocytes with intraepidermal nests of these cells in vacuolated spaces (Pautrier microabscesses). Immunohistochemistry shows CD3+, CD4+, CD8- phenotype. The diagnosis is:
opts: Primary cutaneous CD30+ anaplastic large cell lymphoma
questions.exp: Mycosis fungoides (MF) is the most common primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. It presents with an indolent course through patch, plaque, and tumor stages. Key histological features are epidermotropism and Pautrier microabscesses (intraepidermal clusters of atypical CD4+ T-cells with cerebriform nuclei). Sezary syndrome is the leukemic variant with >1000 Sezary cells/uL in blood.

questions.q: A 42-year-old male presents with intensely pruritic, flat-topped, violaceous polygonal papules on the flexor wrists and Wickham striae visible on buccal mucosa. Biopsy confirms lichen planus. What is the most common site of mucosal involvement in lichen planus?
questions.exp: The oral mucosa is the most commonly affected mucosal site in lichen planus, occurring in 30-70% of patients. Wickham striae (lacy white reticular pattern) on the buccal mucosa is pathognomonic. Oral LP may occur without skin lesions. Erosive oral LP has malignant potential (transformation to SCC in ~1-3%). Genital LP is second most common.

questions.q: A 22-year-old female presents with a 3cm oval, slightly raised, collarette-scaled patch on the right flank (herald patch) 12 days before the appearance of multiple smaller similar lesions on the trunk arranged in a 'Christmas tree' pattern along the lines of Langer. The currently most supported etiology for this condition is:
questions.exp: Pityriasis rosea is currently believed to be caused by reactivation of HHV-6 and/or HHV-7, supported by detection of viral DNA in lesional skin and blood. The herald patch typically precedes the generalized eruption by 1-2 weeks. The eruption follows skin cleavage lines, giving the 'Christmas tree' pattern on the back. It is self-limiting, resolving in 6-8 weeks.

questions.q: A 28-year-old female presents with depigmented patches on the face, neck, and hands. Wood's lamp examination shows brilliant white fluorescence of the depigmented areas. She is otherwise healthy. Which systemic condition is MOST commonly associated with vitiligo?
opts: Autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto's thyroiditis or Graves' disease)
questions.exp: Autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto's thyroiditis and Graves' disease) is the most commonly associated systemic autoimmune disease in vitiligo patients, occurring in 15-30%. Thyroid function tests (TSH, T3, T4) and thyroid autoantibodies (anti-TPO, anti-thyroglobulin) should be screened in all vitiligo patients. Wood's lamp shows brilliant chalk-white fluorescence in vitiligo.

questions.q: A 32-year-old male presents with a well-defined, smooth, circular patch of hair loss 5cm in diameter on the crown. At the periphery, 'exclamation mark' hairs are visible. Nail examination reveals multiple tiny irregular pits on multiple fingernails. Which statement is correct regarding nail changes in alopecia areata?
opts: Onychomycosis (nail fungal infection) is the most common nail change
Nail pitting is the most common nail change, seen in up to 66% of patients
Nail changes never occur in alopecia areata
questions.exp: Nail changes occur in 10-66% of alopecia areata patients. Nail pitting is the most common change and may be the only finding; pits in AA tend to be smaller, shallower, and more regularly distributed than psoriatic pits. Other nail changes include trachyonychia, Beau's lines, onychorrhexis, and red-spotted lunulae. More severe nail changes correlate with more extensive hair loss.

questions.q: A 17-year-old male presents with numerous comedones, inflammatory papules, pustules, and a few nodules on the face and upper back. He has not received prior treatment. According to standard guidelines, the most appropriate first-line regimen for moderate inflammatory acne is:
opts: Oral doxycycline combined with topical benzoyl peroxide
questions.exp: For moderate inflammatory acne, the recommended regimen is an oral antibiotic (doxycycline 50-100mg/day or lymecycline) combined with topical benzoyl peroxide (BPO). BPO is added to prevent/reduce antibiotic resistance. Topical retinoid may be added. Oral isotretinoin is reserved for severe, nodular, or treatment-resistant acne. Intralesional steroids are for individual large nodules/cysts.

questions.q: A 30-year-old male took cotrimoxazole for a UTI. Within 24 hours he develops a well-defined, round, dusky-violaceous edematous plaque with central blistering on the glans penis. It heals with residual hyperpigmentation. Three months later, after taking the same drug, the lesion reappears at exactly the SAME anatomical site. This is characteristic of:
questions.exp: Fixed drug eruption (FDE) is characterized by recurrence at exactly the same site(s) on re-exposure to the causative drug. It heals with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (active lesion is dusky-red/violaceous). Common culprits include cotrimoxazole, NSAIDs, tetracyclines, and metronidazole. The genital area is a classic site.

questions.q: A 21-year-old male develops classic target lesions (three concentric zones: dusky center, pale edematous ring, outer erythematous halo) on the palms and dorsa of hands with minimal oral involvement. He had recurrent herpes labialis one week prior. The most common precipitating cause of recurrent erythema multiforme minor is:
questions.exp: HSV reactivation (both HSV-1 and HSV-2) is responsible for >70% of cases of recurrent erythema multiforme minor. The typical target lesion with three zones is pathognomonic. Mycoplasma pneumoniae is more commonly associated with EM major and atypical SJS (Stevens-Johnson syndrome). Drugs (sulfonamides) are the leading cause of SJS/TEN.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with intensely pruritic, grouped papulovesicles symmetrically distributed on the elbows, knees, sacrum, and buttocks. Biopsy of perilesional skin on direct immunofluorescence shows granular IgA deposits at the tips of dermal papillae. The first-line treatment for this condition is:
opts: Dapsone combined with a strict gluten-free diet
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is the cutaneous manifestation of celiac disease. Granular IgA at dermal papillary tips on DIF is pathognomonic. Dapsone provides rapid (24-48 hour) symptom relief by inhibiting neutrophil function. A strict gluten-free diet is the definitive long-term treatment, addressing the underlying enteropathy and potentially allowing Dapsone tapering over months to years.

questions.q: A newborn develops blistering at sites of minimal trauma on the hands and feet. Electron microscopy of a perilesional skin biopsy shows tissue cleavage occurring below the lamina densa. Immunofluorescence mapping reveals complete absence of type VII collagen at the dermal-epidermal junction. This is consistent with:
questions.exp: In dystrophic EB, mutations in COL7A1 (type VII collagen gene) lead to absent or defective anchoring fibrils below the lamina densa. EM shows cleavage below the lamina densa (sublamina densa). EBS cleavage is intraepidermal (within basal keratinocytes). Junctional EB cleavage is within the lamina lucida (absent laminin-332 or BPAG2). Kindler syndrome has mixed cleavage planes.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman has daily wheals and angioedema for 9 weeks with no identifiable external trigger. Autologous serum skin test (ASST) produces a wheal 2.5mm greater than the saline control at 30 minutes. The significance of a positive ASST in this setting is:
opts: Confirms specific IgE-mediated allergy to a food allergen
Suggests circulating functional autoantibodies against IgE or FcεRIα on mast cells
Indicates physical urticaria triggered by intradermal injection
Diagnoses hereditary angioedema due to C1 inhibitor deficiency
questions.exp: A positive ASST (wheal ≥1.5mm larger than saline control) in chronic spontaneous urticaria suggests autoimmune pathogenesis. The patient's serum contains functional IgG autoantibodies that directly activate mast cells via FcεRIα or cross-link surface IgE, triggering histamine release. This autoimmune subtype affects ~40-50% of CSU patients and may require second-line immunomodulatory treatment (cyclosporine, omalizumab).

questions.q: A 30-year-old male is newly diagnosed with paucibacillary leprosy (3 skin lesions, slit-skin smear negative at all 6 sites). According to the current WHO multidrug therapy (MDT) protocol, the correct treatment regimen for paucibacillary leprosy is:
opts: Rifampicin 600mg once monthly + Dapsone 100mg daily for 12 months
Rifampicin 600mg monthly + Clofazimine 300mg monthly + Dapsone 100mg daily for 12 months
Rifampicin 600mg once monthly + Dapsone 100mg daily for 6 months
questions.exp: WHO MDT for paucibacillary (PB) leprosy: Rifampicin 600mg once monthly (supervised) + Dapsone 100mg daily for 6 months. For multibacillary (MB) leprosy: Rifampicin 600mg monthly + Clofazimine 300mg monthly + Clofazimine 50mg daily + Dapsone 100mg daily for 12 months. Dapsone monotherapy is obsolete due to resistance. PB is defined as 1-5 skin lesions with negative SSS.
